⏺ Terminal multiplexers like tmux and GNU Screen let you run many terminal sessions inside one window and keep
  them alive on their own, separate from the window that shows them. A few practical benefits follow from     
  that.
                                                                                                              
  Sessions that survive disconnects. This is the main reason people use them. If you SSH into a remote server 
  and start a long job, such as a database migration, a big compile or a data-processing script, a dropped
  connection normally kills it. Inside a multiplexer, the session keeps running on the server after the       
  connection drops. You reconnect, reattach, and find everything where you left it, including the scrollback  
  and running processes.                                                                                     
                                                                                                              
  Detach and reattach on purpose. You can also detach deliberately. Start work on your office machine, detach,
  go home, SSH in and pick up the same session. Your editor, shell history and running tasks all stay intact.
                                                                                                         
  Several panes and windows in one terminal. Multiplexers split the screen into panes and group them into     
  windows, like tabs. You might keep an editor in one pane, a test runner in another and live logs in a third,
  all visible together. This works the same way over SSH, where you can't just open more GUI windows on the   
  remote machine.                                                                                             
                                                                                                              
  Named sessions per project. You can keep one named session per project, each with its own layout. Switching 
  projects means switching sessions, without rebuilding your workspace every time.                         
                                                                                                              
  Copy mode and synchronized input. Copy mode lets you scroll back, search and copy text with only the       
  keyboard. Synchronized panes send the same keystrokes to several shells at once, which helps when you run   
  identical commands on many servers.                                       
                                                                                                            
  Scripting and setup. A config file holds your keybindings, status bar and plugins. Scripts can rebuild   
  complex layouts in seconds, and plugins like tmux-resurrect can restore sessions after a reboot.         
                                                                                                             
  In short, multiplexers make terminal work more durable and easier to organize, and they help most on remote 
  machines.
